answer.rationale: With only 14 days to contract expiry and the line running at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer, switching primary supply to the low-cost vendor (memory_c2) carries onboarding and ramp risk that could tip delivery below commitment—an unacceptable trade given the stated objective of minimizing TCO without increasing delivery risk. memory_c4 shows that benchmarking-driven renegotiation with the incumbent recovered real margin and improved payment terms without any supply interruption, and memory_c1 confirms incumbent renewals preserve integration stability. Negotiating terms with the incumbent before expiry addresses the cost mandate pressure while avoiding the qualification/ramp risk of a new primary vendor under a tight, buffer-less production schedule. I verify memory_c4 because it is the load-bearing memory justifying this lower-risk path over the seemingly larger cost win from switching; I want to confirm the original record actually shows margin recovery comparable to the mandate rather than a smaller, rounded-up gain. This does not fully guarantee the 18% target is met by negotiation alone, so that gap and the possibility we may need a second-source or partial switch next cycle should remain flagged rather than treated as resolved.
